idiom_name: Casbin enforcer (model.conf + policy.csv/adapter) consulted from middleware; a role->permission map plus a hierarchy closure for small systems
implementation_notes: The Go answer is Casbin: NewEnforcer("model.conf", "policy.csv") (or a database adapter), then e.Enforce(sub, obj, act) returns the decision; the model file's [role_definition] g = _, _ turns the policy rows into the user-role and role-permission relations, and Enforce carries the hierarchy closure for you. The Go Enforcer is safe for concurrent use, so one instance per process is shared behind a thin middleware that resolves the subject from the authenticated principal (see authenticator) carried in the request context and writes 403 on deny; the policy lives in a file, DB or watcher-backed store and is reloaded with LoadPolicy. For systems too small to want the dependency, the honest hand-rolled form is map[Role]map[Permission]bool plus a role-hierarchy edge set closed once at load, with roles read from context and a deny-by-default guard - an interface plus map that mirrors the pattern's four relations without the library.
pitfalls: Ignoring the error from Enforce turns an enforcement failure into a silent allow; treat any error as deny.
Reading roles or a subject ID from query parameters, form fields or headers the session never verified lets a caller widen its own permissions; use the authenticated principal only.
Calling LoadPolicy on the hot path reloads the whole store per request; reload on a watcher or interval and let Enforce read the shared, thread-safe model.
Granting a permission straight to a user (a p, alice, ... policy row) instead of through a role bypasses the reviewable matrix.
Omitting the [role_definition] g line makes role rows inert - every role check denies - so exercise the model file with a test carrying a known allow case.
